utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Unfortunately, the other Trial Chamber was a little delayed so this start has been consequently delayed. I apologise. Mr. Lukic. And, Mr. Sljivancanin, you will remember that the affirmation still applies that you took.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the interpreters can hear me well. This courtroom is always a problem. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to all in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, once again, Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope that we will finish within one hour and that really depends on your cooperation. Please give me answers that are as brief as possible. I will just focus on certain subjects that were dealt with by Mr. Moore and my colleagues from the Defence. So let's deal with this quickly because I'm sure that you also want to relax a bit and to get this over with. First, I'm going to put a question to you that Mr. Vasic asked you about on the first day. He asked you about that entry in the war diary of the 80th Kragojevac Brigade, dated the 19th; 375, I think it was. I don't think we should put it on the screen. I think you know it. It says that a surrender is expected of the Ustasha forces in the area of the hospital. My question is the following: Do you know that, during the course of those few days, there ever was a surrender of the ZNGs, the MUP, the Ustasha forces - I'm not sure what the exact use of the term was - in the area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the area of the hospital. There was no surrender ever in the area of Vukovar, except for those who surrendered at Mitnica. There were no other surrenders.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 31st of October, that is to say, the second day of your cross-examination, the Prosecutor asked you - this is page 15 of the working transcript; I'm sorry not to have compared it to the official pages - but he asked you about certain facts, that you asked soldiers from the front line to tell you what the situation was there, the morale, and so on and so forth. Do you remember that the Prosecutor asked you about this? So my question would be as follows: The dissemination of misinformation or false information about the situation in the units, about the situation at the front line, betrayals of officers, intentional misfiring and misshelling, is that the task of a security organ in the sense of article 6(D), where you are in charge of that particular duty in terms of this basic work conducted by security organs, to see what the actual state of affairs is due to your very own job?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood it then and now, all of that had to do with hostile activity within the unit and vis-a-vis the unit. I am correcting you - I don't know whether the Prosecutor put it that way - I did not seek information. As I moved about in the units of the Guards Brigade, I talked to people and to soldiers. On the basis of talking to them, I concluded whether this information, from the conversations I had with them, was important in terms of security.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this was discussed in units, that there was betrayal, that there is defeatism, that people don't want to go to the front, that combat planning was not done right, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such discussions even before we set out to accomplish this task, and at the place where the task was being carried out. And I said that I thought then that perhaps we, the command, made a mistake then, because we allowed people to receive mail, letters. Even at the very front line they got this mail, and their family members were writing to them. Everybody was afraid for Yugoslavia then, whether it would survive, whether it would not survive, and that affected us, the members of the Yugoslav People's Army, the most, us who loved this country. People probably took this very badly and this affected them, and they were wavering psychologically and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you twice, the first day and yesterday, I believe, about using the term "Ustasha" and you gave an answer in relation to this. My question is as follows: Do you remember whether, at that time, in the official documents of Mr. Zivota Panic, and from the 1st Army, and from the institutions in charge, from the Federal Secretary for National Defence, as for the Croat forces, if I can put it that way, was the term "Ustasha" used in official documents; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that this term was used, but my understanding was at the time that that only pertained to those who took up arms and joined the paramilitary formations in order to fight against members of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please show Exhibit 729, page 2, on the screens. Can it be zoomed in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to read the first paragraph. This is a Prosecution document. This is a commendation, a citation, sent by Veljko Kadijevic, Federal Secretary, to the units that took part in the Vukovar operation. "Carrying out their tasks in repelling attacks at units and facilities of the JNA and preventing a repetition of genocide and other consequences of interethnic armed conflicts, the armed forces of Yugoslavia achieved major success in combat operations in the area of Vukovar. In long and difficult fighting, elite Ustasha forces were defeated taken prisoner, as well as many murderers from home and abroad." Were you aware of this document? And the second question: In the public media at that time, was the term "Ustasha" often used for these formations of the other side, that is to say, the paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this document, I cannot recall right now, but probably the assistant commander for moral guidance dealt with this, if it had to do with our unit, too. This is a document from the cabinet of the Federal Secretary. I explained earlier on that at that time, my understanding of the term "Ustasha" was that it was used by them, themselves, those who were opposed to us, who were on the other side in relation to us. Considering there was only those paramilitary formations --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You explained that. Let's not repeat that. Do you remember whether those terms were used in the media?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were used every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I would like to ask that the witness be shown that set of Prosecution tabs that was used the first day, military documents and the rest. I would like to have a look for a moment. That is Exhibit 847.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, the B/C/S version, tab 12. And for the Trial Chamber and the OTP, it is tab 11. Mr. Moore asked you about this document. Could you please look at page 2, please. Three pieces of information are referred to here that you testified about during your examination-in-chief, stating that this is information that you provided to the cabinet of the SSNO, that is to say, further on, to the security administration. The first is Bibic Milan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down. The interpreters cannot follow. The witness answered "correct" to all three questions, and all three names were not heard by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The first information is Milan Bibic, the second information is Boro Bugunovic, and the third information is about Muharem Besic. Could you please look at page 1 now, the very beginning of the text. The first sentence or the first few words, that is what I am going to state: "Several sources of the security organs of the JNA indicate that at crisis areas," and so on and so forth. This document, was it compiled only on the basis of your information or some other information? Sorry for phrasing the question that way, but I have to.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said on that day, and I'm saying now, that one source of information was the information provided by the security organ that I was in charge of. So in our reports, we precisely wrote about these three persons that you mentioned here, and I believe that we were one of the sources of information. I already explained: A security organ never deals only with one source. In order to be able to bring criminal charges against a person, as a security organ, or to suspect a person of having committed a criminal offence, I have to be certain of that and I have to have several sources of information, several pieces of information, unless a person was caught red-handed, so to speak. It was very hard, this work of ours, and a great deal of effort had to be made in order to prove that a person had committed a crime. So it is not only my information that is taken into account, but several information at that. I do apologise. May I just add something else? That is why this document was returned to me from the cabinet of the chief of the General Staff, recommending that I document the activity taken by these persons. I said, if this minister said -- that this minister left the territory once this was made known.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, there is no doubt about that. We've already discussed that. That is why I'd like us to deal with very concrete subjects during this re-direct. There is no need to repeat what you've already said. As for this document and the allegations made, if I can put it that way, or rather, what you said about Besic Muharem, I see in the last paragraph that the security administration is asking the command of the 1st Military District to set up a commission. Why? There you go. In two words, can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the gentleman was from the units that belonged to the 1st Military District. As for the work of this gentleman, we documented what he was doing, because it says here what is attached, that is to say, that we found the authorisations that he had issued and we sent this as a document with his signature. And that is why a commission was set up, to see what was going on. And what happened to him later is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the first page of this document, Mr. Moore showed you a sentence where the plural is used for "prisoners" that are being brutally treated, and increasingly, often, they are being killed in order to meet out justice that way. In addition to this case, throughout your stay in Vukovar, did you here of any such incident of that nature, that prisoners were treated brutally and that they were being killed, in the plural, as it says here?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document applies to the entire territory of the entire military district, or perhaps of the territory of all Yugoslavia, because it was written by the security administration. In my report, there aren't any such reports except such references. Had I heard of that, I would have written about it, as I wrote about these people. If I didn't write about it, then I didn't know about that. I wrote about my own zone, and this was written about the territory of all of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you are coming in very quickly; Mr. Sljivancanin is responding to you very quickly and at high speed. The interpreters will just not be able to maintain this pace, so we must slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for the umpteenth time to the interpreters. My wish is to control the witness, so to speak, so once I get the answer that I'm seeking, I don't want to him to engage in repetition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Sljivancanin, that is perhaps why I am interrupting you, that is why I am interjecting. But I would really just like to discuss what I am interested in. I do apologise. During combat activity in Vukovar, did you ever receive security information or instructions from the organ, the security organ of the 1st Military District; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single piece of information from the security organ of the 1st Military District. I never received a single one while I was in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Vukovar, did you send any information, seek suggestion or advice or whatever, from the security organs of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not seek any assistance and I did not send any information. As I already explained, I sent all information to the persons I mentioned here, or rather, the professional organ in charge that was giving me information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please move on to tab 10 now, that is to say, the information from Colonel Jeremija. That is 9 for the Trial Chamber; 636 is the exhibit number. Mr. Moore put a question to you and he expounded on his own thesis that there was widespread mistreatment of Croat forces and that there was significant documentation corroborating that. He said that on the 31st of October and he showed this document to you. You already testified during the examination-in-chief that you did not hear of the Lovas case while in Vukovar. While you were here in detention, or when you had the opportunity of seeing your own documentation and the documentation of the Prosecution, did you see any other document, report, information, that speaks of mistreatment or abuse of Croat forces, except for this Lovas case, that would jog your memory, remind you that, perhaps, you are aware of some other such case? Did you see any other evidence?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any other evidence. To be quite clear, I think I saw this telegram here. I heard someone mention it here, perhaps, too. I saw it here in the courtroom. I did not see any other evidence, ever. The mentioned gentleman wrote this probably for his own zone, so it could not have referred to anything that was widespread, only if he saw it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you, I think this was on the 31st and, once again, yesterday, as to what you did when Major Vukasinovic informed you about the events in the barracks, when he returned the bus with 24 persons on board. My question is the following: Try to look back to the past and those days in Vukovar. In your assessment as the chief of security of the Guards Brigade, on the 20th of November, 1991, which facility was the safest in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Guards Brigade had come to Vukovar and entered the barracks, for me, the safest and securest facility was that facility, and that is where I felt best as a soldier, that is, in the barracks. The barracks were a facility that provided peace for everyone and especially soldiers who were on assignment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you aware what forces Captain Predojevic's company had, what forces he had at his disposal to secure the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was well aware of that. That company had previously secured the headquarters, so it didn't have many casualties. It had three platoons and each platoon had three armoured personnel carriers, and the crew of one carrier was eight to ten men. So I cannot tell you by heart the exact strength of the whole unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is superior to the security officers in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the security of the barracks, it is the barracks commander who is in charge in every respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who is the commander of Predojevic's company?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That company, once it entered Vukovar, became part of the 2nd Advanced Detachment, it was resubordinated to it. And the battalion commander was Kavalic and then he was replaced by Mr. Susic, that is, the assault detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where his command post was those days? Where was he stationed at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd rather not engage in any guesswork. I really can't remember where the command post was of the command of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Never mind. Let me ask you something else. You testified that you asked Mr. Vukasinovic who was there and that he informed you that Major Lukic was that, or rather, lieutenant colonel. What was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Lieutenant Colonel Lukic was sent by the commander to assist the commander of the 2nd Motorised Battalion, and for a while, he was barracks commander. And I testified to that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was Lieutenant Colonel Panic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Panic was Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of this information which you obtained from Mr. Vukasinovic, were you able to make a security assessment regarding the risk these people were exposed to? Did you act in that sense and assess whether you need to go there and intervene?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knowing these officers and knowing the situation in the barracks up until then, there was no need for me to go or to undertake anything at all, because these were highly responsible officers. So they would be entitled to give me assignments rather than me giving them assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see now Exhibit 107, page 16 in the B/C/S and page 20 of the English text. It is article 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, Mr. Moore asked you several times about - let me put it in simple terms - whether you were superior to Borisavljevic as the security organ of the 80th Kragujevac Brigade; that you were the main person for security in the territory of the operative group.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we enlarge this article 49, please. The page was fine, page 16. Article 49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read the second paragraph: "Data which constitute an official secret. The officer from para 1 of this article may inform other authorised officers of the security organ or other persons about them only upon authority from the superior officer of the security organ." Who, in your opinion, was the superior officer?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My superior officer was the chief of the security of the Federal Secretary for Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Vukosavljevic, who was the superior officer to him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security of the corps to which that brigade belongs, I think that was the 24th Corps, according to the testimony I heard here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you exchange information without permission of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain here that all activities of security organs are confidential and secret. That is why we had closed sessions and I hesitated to speak about things in public. Even security organs do not share the information amongst themselves but only with their superiors along the chain of command. I did not take part in that discussion much for that particular reason when we were in open session. Do you wish us to go into closed session for this purpose?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we have time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of discussion about those lists in the binder. While we have this tab in front of you, please look at tab 22, Exhibit 834. The English version is tab 21. This is your report addressed to the security organ of the cabinet of the Federal Secretary of National Defence on the 9th of November, 1991. Please look at page 2 and the last sentence of the last paragraph. I'll read it to you: "We are expecting that further combat operations will generate more such people and we, therefore, request that you send us any new information about all the extremists in the Vukovar area and the vicinity for further intelligence work." Will you now please look at the other set of documents - could the usher assist, please? - the other binder known as the lists. Tab 6, Mr. Sljivancanin, please. Tab 5, Exhibit 826, page 1, please. This is a letter from the institution you wrote to, dated the 10th of November, 1991, and it is addressed to you, and it has to do with the lists that Mr. Moore discussed with you. But I'm going to read you this first. It says here -- the title is "Intelligence on Members of the Zengas, the Croatian National Guard Corps, and the Ministry of the Interior in Vukovar," and then it says: "Based on general intelligence from the Federal Secretariat of National Defence and the security administration, the Republic of Serbia MUP and the security organ of the cabinet, we have selected some partially-verified intelligence and are sending them for your use. Although some of the intelligence is no longer relevant, it can be used to determine focal points for searches on the ground, controlling liberated territory, and potentially for finding concealed members of the MUP and the Zengas, as well as for questioning prisoners of war." Mr. Sljivancanin, before the question, look at the previous binder again, the one we were looking at a moment ago, and let us look now at Exhibit 835, tab 24. For Your Honours, tab 25. It is a report of the same body, with the same date, addressed to the security administration. And I'm reading the first paragraph: "We are hereby sending you the report of the security organ of the Guards Brigade upon which we acted and took the necessary measures of guidance primarily concerning the efficient organisation of work with prisoners of war. We have sent more recent information and knowledge and the information of the security administration, and we are currently carrying out identity checks in accordance with information gathered in interviews." My question to you is: These three documents, as I have placed them before you, are they in a certain order, following one another, whereby you are reporting on what is happening with respect to those persons and the influx in terms of the liberation of the Bosko Buha settlement? You're asking for information for your operative intelligence work, and then your superior is sending you information from the security administration and other sources, informing the administration of the same. Have I properly understood this?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have fully explained this, and that is why I asked that all these documents be tendered such as they are, whereas only details are read out that may be in somebody's interest. I believe that Their Honours will read these documents in detail. If I may just add with respect to these lists. When a large group of civilians appear, for us, as the security organ, there are persons who want to admit if they have done something and then it is easy to gain information; there are others who conceal themselves. So we didn't go there to sit around; as the security organ, we went to work there. And those who committed crimes should be arraigned and handed over to the investigators. These lists are not all significant for me, but if a certain person under a certain name appears among this group, I have to forward him to the investigator. It is easier to proceed in this way rather than suspecting each and every civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you, as the security organ, get instructions and information about persons that you need to find or about whom you need to collect information, do you make an omission if you allow such persons to hide and escape?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. This is a very serious omission on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor put it to you that some persons for whom you received information, or rather, that they are mentioned in the indictment as persons whose bodies were found or are registered as missing, but at any rate, that, in his view, they are among the people who were taken out of the hospital on the 20th of November. Now, in your view, where were these persons supposed to be taken on the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All persons who were brought in as crime suspects were supposed to be taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that fully in line with what was stated by Mr. Kypr in his talks with Colonel Pavkovic, in Exhibits 320 and 333, that General Raseta ordered that wounded members of the National Guards Corps would not be allowed to leave Vukovar in the convoy of the wounded. You saw that document.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it. That is the decision of the Superior Command and it was in line with what had been decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few questions about Velepromet. Mr. Moore claims that you isolated people there. My question is: Was that isolation or was that temporary detention until their identity was established, whether these persons belonged to the category that you were supposed to be dealing with, as security organ?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never any isolation. These people who were kept for interviews were not kept for longer than two or three hours with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You or your security organs, could you order anything to Zigic, Jaksic, Ljubinko Stojanovic, or any other TO leader?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't even try to give them any orders. We were just making suggestions if anything was needed. They were given orders through their chain of command. I tried to explain to you that the security organ is not supposed to interfere with the chain of command or the command if they want to carry out their task successfully. Any security organ that interferes will not carry out his professional duties, specialist duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me not be too literal, but could they issue any orders to you, these three people from the TO?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not order us to do anything. They could not issue any kind of orders to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown Mr. Schou's evidence and you remember yourself, you were in the courtroom, that on the 19th of November, you forbade the International Red Cross to enter the hospital; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see please Exhibit 333 on the screen. B/C/S page 3. The title is "Comments and Lessons." Page 3. I think that the English is there, too. A bit lower down, please. "Comments and Lessons," number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says -- I'm reading the second paragraph: "During the evacuation in Vukovar, we were forbidden, on the evening before the evacuation, to meet with the administration of the hospital through an order issued by Admiral Brovet through our liaison officer with the JNA." This is a document of the head of the European Monitors, Colonel Calaghan. We have a document here that we don't want to show here. May I refresh your memory: Discussions are taking place on that day, and we know who the liaison officer for the JNA was. It says here that Memisevic, Loncar and Lazarevic [as interpreted] were the liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question: Were you ever a liaison officer of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I was never liaison officer. And I wish to clarify what you read out. I, as security officer, everything I did with the European monitors, I did only when the liaison officer asked me to do that. These liaison officers were the most important people who took care of this, and they received instructions from those who brought them in. Not a single delegation could come without a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correction: On page 18, line 25, the third officer referred to in that document was Major Zaric, not Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that everybody in this courtroom knows this, but can you tell us, nevertheless, who was Admiral Brovet, and what position did he have then?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Assistant Federal Secretary for National Defence, Admiral Brovet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we're dealing with this document, the Prosecutor also asked you about Schou's report, this evacuation of the wounded that Schou describes in his report, that there were no priorities involved in terms of the wounded and the staff. Remember that you were asked about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we go back to page 2, now, of this document, the same document. So there is just one page --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I didn't object to the earlier approach to a document that I had not used. I have no objection to the use of the document, but it is the content of the document. The witness, surely, should be asked whether, in actual fact, as should have been, I submit, on the last occasion, why was it you refused Schou to go to the hospital, rather than showing the document and basically leading the witness. I would submit, if there is an issue, the witness can be asked about it; and if there is confirmation of it, then that is open for the Defence to use. But to use the document to refresh the memory and then ask for confirmation, in my submission, is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. It's a trap that counsel on all sides have fallen into during this trial. Mr. Lukic, if you could watch out for it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just make a small comment. Of course I will be careful, but I think, after all, that Mr. Sljivancanin does not belong to the category of witnesses who - how should I put it? - is not aware of all documents in detail. I think that he has been testifying here for quite a few days now. He testified, and he said even during his examination-in-chief, that he himself did not stop the representatives of the international community on the 19th of November. He is very well aware of this document. But there's no problem with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sljivancanin, first I'm going to ask you as follows, my question is: As for the wounded, you talked about that a bit to Mr. Moore and you said that it was mostly the soldiers who were carrying the wounded. What about the wounded being taken into the medical vehicles and when the convoy set out for Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when the column or convoy came, led by Mr. Pavkovic, that he called Major Tesic and asked soldiers to help load the wounded into the vehicles, and I know that it was the military doctors who were in charge of that and part of the staff were helping from the medical centre, part of them only, because many of them ran into the buses. I really was not in charge of that. I was not engaged in any one of those assignments. But what I saw the most was that it was soldiers who were carrying the wounded into those vehicles, as the doctors in the hospital were telling them how each wounded person should be carried.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm very briefly going to read out one sentence and I'm going to ask you whether this refreshes your memory, that this is the way it actually went, the way the report says. And this is what it says -- this is a report of Mr. Calaghan's group of the European monitors: "The wounded who could walk, the elderly and children, got out of the hospital as a mass that could not be kept under control. Most of the old administration, instead of helping with the evacuation of the hospital or instead of caring for the wounded, were sitting in front of the complex, the hospital complex, not doing anything. The ambulances had problems with reaching the entrance of the hospital where there were masses of staff, and in this way, they were practically hindering the placement of wounded persons into ambulances."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before you said this and read this out, I testified about that. Everybody just tried to run into the buses, and that is why I said that I was proud of my soldiers, my young soldiers, who behaved that way, who carried the wounded who had been shooting at them until the previous day. You can play this recording and you can see. Well, the man wrote it the way it was. He probably wrote the truth, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for what Mr. Schou said, that the International Red Cross was prevented from entering the hospital on the 19th - that is quite literally what he said and what he wrote in his report - I'm going to ask you the following: You know, you remember, the detailed testimony of Mrs. Bosanac - that is page 686 - when she testified, stating that she insisted that Borsinger should stay there and spend the night there, and that he quite literally said that he had nothing to do there and that he would come in the morning. Were you present, perhaps? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very well. That is correct. Mr. Borsinger, when I also asked him to go and look at the corpses together, and Paunovic told me that they were there - yesterday, these corpses were shown on the screens - he told me that he had this very important business to attend to that could not be postponed. And he apologised to me and to Dr. Bosanac, saying that he had to go. Of course, I didn't ask him where he had to go and why he was in such a hurry. But, anyway, I asked him for the medicine to be brought to the hospital, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asserts on the 1st of November, on page 76, rather, he said that the group of Bogdan Vujic, if I can call them that, came to help you. You said that there's an entry in the war diary about that, as to what their task was. Now I'm going to ask that this be placed on the screens, but let me ask you: Do you remember what their task was; to help you or something else?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they came to help us, and the entry in the war diary does say exactly what their assignment was and why they came. I'm saying here now as well that that is precisely why they came, to carry out this assignment, to carry out the triage of perpetrators of crimes that were supposed to be taken to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please place on the screens now Exhibit 401, the war diary. In B/C/S, it's page 48; in English, it's 41. The 19th of November, at 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before this is placed on the screen, may I say that, as far as I know, the rules of service in the armed forces of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that applied to the JNA, assignments were given very precisely to officers as to who was supposed to do what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 48, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the way it is. I'm going to read it. The 19th of November, at 2000 hours, this is what it says: "A team from the security organs has arrived in the area of responsibility of the OG South to select and separate members of the Ustasha formations from civilians." The next entry, the same handwriting, I see it's Trifunovic - I assume it's Trifunovic - the 20th of November, at 0100 hours: "A team from the logistical organs of the 1st Military District has arrived to help with security and transport of the civilians, the wounded and sick." Is there a difference between the two entries in terms of vocabulary? I don't want to lead in any way.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a big difference. I think that since this gentleman, as far as I can see, was probably Trifunovic, he wasn't just writing all this off the top of his head of. He wrote this on the basis of the authorisation he got from the task of the leader of that group. And what you asked about logistics, this assistance that is referred to, that means that we do not have motor vehicles of our own that are needed. Probably there has to be mobilisation of such vehicles or, I don't know, from work organisations, whatever, to get buses that the JNA did not have among its own resources in order to transport the people who were supposed to be transported. So the difference is a major one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore suggested to you that it was illogical for Mr. Vujic already then, at that meeting, to propose that you meet the next morning in front of Velepromet, because he had just arrived. But, anyway, that was what he was asserting. Now I'm asking you the following: At that time, or rather, first of all, do you remember how many persons were in that group?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three high officers with the rank of colonel are the people I remember. I remember there were other officers, too. And to tell you the truth, I cannot remember the actual number now, but I'm sure that three were sitting at the table. But now I cannot remember to say whether there were nine, ten, five of them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. You know what Vujic's testimony was, that Mr. Korica, Mosesku, Muncan were there, and so on, not to go into all the names. At that time, when you were discussing this, to go to Velepromet, that that was a priority, did you know that the work at Velepromet would be completed that night?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. Based on the information I had from my security officer, Captain Borisavljevic, and because it was dark, I believed that there would be enough work there for the entire following day, during daytime. That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anybody there that there was enough work there for the following day?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed them in detail that evening about everything that I knew at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next topic: Mr. Moore asked you whether you ever supported the political doctrine of Mr. Seselj, and to that end he put a portion of your interview from 1996 to you. In that interview of yours, did you speak of the political doctrine of Mr. Seselj or did you speak of his position vis-a-vis the JNA, whose member you were?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never accepted Mr. Seselj as a politician. I only see him as a comical figure who appears at a scene, in a theatre, or something like that. I never discussed his political doctrine at all. I wasn't interested in it. And if a journalist wrote something, perhaps this journalist wrote about what suited him. I was never interested in Mr. Seselj's political doctrine, and I can state it loud and clear. I stated so back then and I can state it now. As for the papers, they report on everything. And perhaps I simply stated what I had heard from Mr. Vuk Obradovic about Seselj having a positive attitude towards the JNA. But other than that, I no nothing further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any conflicts with Mr. Seselj at that period of time, with him and with his supporters?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this can be called a conflict, although we had no direct contact, then yes, we had a conflict at the House of Flowers in 1996, or in 1991, when they wanted to knock down the grave of Comrade Tito. That was the conflict I had with them, or rather, we, members of the Guards Brigade, had with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was one of your tasks prescribed by the very existence of the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our tasks were always very clear and accurate: We were there to secure the grave of Comrade Tito. We were to ensure that it remained intact, and as long as we secured it, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go, for a moment, into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask Mr. Lukic to turn off his microphone while the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moore put to you something that you said during examination-in-chief about the evidence of Mrs. Zvesdana Polovina, about where the men were supposed to go, you know, those who were supposed to go to the barracks for questioning; and then you said that what you had stated to her at the time wasn't true. My question is: Did you ever prevent anyone from learning where that group of buses had gone to when the convoy for the transportation of the wounded arrived? And by this, I mean international representatives, the JNA officers who were there, journalists. And, finally, did you prevent civilians who were present there from talking to them?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not prevent; not only I, but no other member of the Guards Brigade in that area did that. To the contrary, I had -- rather, I always instructed people and gave them information about where they were. I mostly instructed them to go to Velepromet. And everybody who had been taken away as a suspect, my suggestion was that they needed to be taken to Sremska Mitrovica, to the prison there. So that was the information that I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Would you please make sure that your answers are brief. Now I'm going to turn to a different topic. The Prosecutor put it to you that the members of the TO who were armed were a real threat in terms of revenge; do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were the members of the TO armed throughout the conflict while you were there? Did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived, they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And please tell me, throughout your stay there, did you observe a single case where the members of the TO manifested a desire for revenge?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard anything of the sort, and wherever I moved, I never saw a single person who was bent on revenge or attempted to do that. Let me just supplement my answer. In every case where we had any doubts, as I stated in my report, then we disarmed such people, even though we were allowed to use these people to reinforce our own units. And you can read about this in my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a brief question about the article which appeared in "Monitor." I'm not going to call it an interview, relying on your words that it wasn't an interview that you authorised. You covered this quite in detail with Mr. Moore and I will just have one brief question about it for you. This interview dates from late 1992. In the previous period of time, did you give any interviews to public media houses, and were these interviews available to everyone?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we were to analyse in depth what an interview is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I talked to journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We may proceed. Now we're going to turn to the statement that you gave to the security administration. Maybe we should take the relevant binder with statements. Let us turn to page 5 of this statement you gave to the security administration where you discuss Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is tab 1 of the binder where the statements are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Moore -- this is quoted on page 76 of yesterday's transcript. Mr. Moore suggested to you that, based on this statement, Vukasinovic told you that it wasn't nice to mistreat those people at Ovcara, and that, in his view, that could not have happened on the 19th - that's Mr. Moore's position - that it had to be on the 20th; and that Vukasinovic told you this in relation to the people who were at Ovcara on the 20th. My question is: In that statement of yours, it says explicitly in the middle of that paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please refer the interpreters to the relevant paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- it says: "I heard from one person it is possible that this involved Major Vukasinovic, although I'm not sure about that, that it wasn't nice to mistreat those people." And that later on you said that everything was peaceful there. This statement was given eight years after the events, as you stated yourself, when you had no information, no documents on you; you didn't have the war diary or anything else that you had heard in the meantime. Did you state to them explicitly in this statement that it was Vukasinovic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't tell them this firmly. I couldn't remember all of the people. And this interview took the whole day. Mr. Moore didn't allow me to say this yesterday, but there are a lot of mistakes in that statement. For example, it says that the commander of the 80th Brigade was Slobodan Misevic, that that's what I said. That was a mistake. And I couldn't remember all of the people and all of the events at the time. I didn't say that I was sure that it was Vukasinovic at the time; I said that it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You heard evidence given by Vojinovic, Vukosavljevic, Bezmarevic, Danilovic, P014, and I think that you read another seven to eight, if not ten, statements given by members of that unit when they testified before the court in Belgrade. All of them, except for P014, stated firmly that you were not at Ovcara on the 20th. You know that because you could read it in the documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I read.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: P014 testified before this Court, stating that he did not see you at Ovcara on the 20th. My question: Did you contact any of these people before 1998 or after 1998?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before 1998, I didn't contact any of these people. As for P014, I contacted that person - let me think - maybe in 2001 or 2000, and I can describe the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't have to. Did you discuss Ovcara at all on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to put my final question to you: Yesterday, at the very end of cross-examination, based on the statement that you gave in front of the hospital where you said that you were proud that you were at the helm of these soldiers and officers - and then we also know that you said to Borsinger that you were the commander in your own country - and Mr. Moore put to you that all of that taken together meant that you were the captain of the ship. My question to you is: During these three years that you have been deeply involved in this case - and you received, continuously, documents both from the Defence and the OTP - did the Prosecution or the Defence provide to you any sort of a document, or did Mr. Moore, in cross-examination, offer to you any document or any regulation that would support that you had the command role in Vukovar in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody supplied such a document to me, nor did I ever see one, nor do I believe that such a document exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Mr. Sljivancanin, do you really think it's important for you to add something?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's important for me to add that, in that interview, I wasn't going to say that I was at the back of the column of my soldiers. No, I mean, what kind of an officer would I be? Because the officer always has to be at the helm, at the head of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked you about this document. Did Mr. Moore ever provide such a document confirming that you were in charge? And, as for 1991 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Lukic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN SLJIVANCANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I was in a proper army that abided by all the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, that's fine, Mr. Sljivancanin. I have concluded my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did the interpreters get your question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat my question. I repeat just the question. "In 1991, were you a member of the army which abided by the regulations?" And Mr. Sljivancanin gave his answer. Thank you, Your Honours. And I apologise, once again, to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Sljivancanin, you will be pleased to know that that concludes the examination of you and the evidence that you have chosen to give, so if you would return to your place. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I thank you for having the patience to listen to me throughout all these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an additional ten minutes. Should we do now what I suggested earlier or should we do it after the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be wonderful to hear you now, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Your Honour starts on that, we just got an e-mail in relation to that application and Mr. Lunny will be dealing with it, so I wonder if -- well, perhaps we can start, but I'd like Mr. Lunny to be in court for that, if it's possible, as he's dealing specifically with the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you saying Mr. Lunny is on his way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I suspect Mr. Lunny is on his way, but I haven't got a tracking device. I'm hoping he's on his way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Borovic, would it trouble you if we waited until after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume again at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The three documents that have been provided to Your Honours is just in support of what I will be saying, and the Prosecution has already been informed, an e-mail with the document and an address to Mr. Smith in connection with all these documents. Your Honours, the Prosecution, in its response to the Defence submission on the adoption of documents with regard to witnesses P018, P022, P024, has pointed out the following: All this reduced to quotations from Rule 54 and Rule 89(C) and (D), and essentially the right to the admission of this evidence is challenged because we did not indicate when we came into possession of these documents. That is one point. And second, why we didn't recall witness P024 for another examination and why, under Rule 22 bis -- 92 bis, sorry, we didn't take a statement from Witness Radovanovic, a physician who signed one of those medical documents. Before I elaborate the position of the Defence, the documents linked to Witness P022, we will withdraw that submission because we showed this witness all the court documents, the witness read parts of the sentence, and I believe that that will be enough for the Chamber regarding the reasons why we wanted to have those documents admitted. We are now talking only about Witness P018 and P024. Referring to the objections of the Prosecution, I am now talking about the court document linked to Witness P024. Under 1, the identity of that witness was disclosed to us late, as a Defence team, we have had problems with witnesses with protective measures, because to gain any kind of documents is a problem; and to explain to judiciary and prosecution institutions why we are asking for such documents is very complicated, because I'm not allowed to say that I will be using those documents in The Hague. So we worked on this very carefully. We didn't have much time, because the witness, P024, started to testify on the 10th of February, 2006. On the 13th of February -- sorry, on the 14th of February, at 7.00 p.m. - and, Your Honours, you have this e-mail - we received information about the sentence for KZ, a number from Sremska Mitrovica, 602/03, from which it can be seen that this witness was sentenced to one year in prison. It was a final decision. Towards the end of the working day, on the 15th of February, I showed the witness this court decision and the case number, and I cannot believe that the witness, who has taken an oath in this Tribunal, lied that this sentence, which is a judicial sentence of a public nature, doesn't exist and that he is not aware of it. He said this because he didn't wish to disclose that an international arrest warrant has been issued against him on the basis of a sentence from the year 2004. Witness P024, Your Honours, on pages 4409 to 4411, on those pages, I explained in detail what is contained in the sentence, so I'll just read out a couple of sentences, not to tire you. My question as the Defence counsel was: "Is it true to say that the district prosecutor invested -- filed an appeal that a higher court in Sremska Mitrovica bar its sentence KZ 602/03, dated the 5th of April, 2004, changed, amended the original decision and sentenced the accused to one year in prison? "No, that is not true," says the witness. "I wasn't there at the time." My second question was, "Did you serve your sentence in Serbia?" The witness said, "No." I also showed him, in the order I have described to the Chamber, "Why did you ask for protective measures? Was it because of secret services you spoke about over the past three days, or was it because you wanted to avoid a prison sentence of one year?" Then you have his monologue and his reply to that question. Therefore, Your Honours, I showed the witness everything I could at that point in time, and if his answer was no, there would be no point in calling him once again for additional examination for him to comment on these court sentences. I then showed the witness that a large number of criminal proceedings were conducted against him, not only for one act of impermissible trade but also for ownership of weapons, which is punishable under the appropriate law, for the criminal act of serious robbery; therefore, several such criminal acts committed in Bosnia when he was looting the houses of refugees, of poor people, the elderly, and women who were still there. And when he wanted to avoid criminal responsibility, he fled to Serbia. These documents arrived from Bosnia, in Serbia, and he was sentenced to one year in prison. I don't want to dwell on this. He was shown that he was suspected of attempted murder, and the punishment for this is 5 to 15 years' imprisonment. You will see in his statement that this was light injury, and his answers were vague, but the truth is that he tried to kill his wife with an axe and she protected her head with her arms and she was very seriously injured. When the Prosecution says that this could not be admitted into evidence by saying that it is a criminal investigation, but this is not a criminal investigation. This is something that has been judged in court and a sentence passed of one year in prison. To avoid any repetition, I showed this to the witness and he commented on all these facts. On the other hand, this Defence team for Miroslav Radic has endeavored to economise with the time. Let us imagine if, for each witness, about whom we subsequently acquire documents and learn information subsequently and then call him back, this would take up a great deal of time. It would not contribute to efficiency. Furthermore, Your Honours, you have the last e-mail among the three documents I have shown you. The very next day, after what happened when examining Witness P024 with colleague Smith, we agreed that he would not oppose the tendering of these documents, as these are court judgements, and one document relating to Witness P018, which is an official document of the Military Medical Academy and it relates to the testimony of P018. Mr. Smith tried to check this, and after some time he asked me to give him the addresses and telephone numbers of the persons who were in the trial chamber for this case, and I have provided that in this e-mail. And Mr. Smith said, if anything should be in dispute, he would let me know; if not, he would not object. I'm sorry, but deputy prosecutors often change on the opposite bench, so if they haven't been informed, this is something we can deal with easily. In paragraph 12 of their filing, the Prosecution asked how we obtained, or rather, when we obtained these documents, and with the help of these faxes and e-mails, I have explained that the dates are the 14th, 15th and 16th of February, 2006. The Trial Chamber - and perhaps this is the most important point I wish to make - in its decision on the Defence submission linked to protective measures for Witness P024, on the 13th of July, 2006, presented a position, which was fully accepted by the Defence, saying that the contradictions and lack of precision in the testimony of this witness is of obvious importance and will be of relevance when Your Honours judge the reliability of this witness. When talking about contradictions, it is a contradiction between what he said and what is contained in the documents. Therefore, Your Honours, for you to be able to judge these contradictions, it is almost impossible to do that unless these documents are admitted into evidence. I think that is all I have to say with respect to Witness P024, as this has been elaborated in our submission on protective measures. Allow me now, briefly, to comment on the document for Witness P018. It is a document of the Military Medical Academy which says that this witness was never on the 14th floor, which houses the neuropsychiatric ward of the Military Medical Academy. The files of medical institutions are classified, according to the law in Serbia, and through the National Council, we managed to obtain this document, addressed to the lawyer's office, and it is an official document, with the stamp of the doctor -- I'm sorry, not the court stamp, the medical stamp, confirming that what he has written is true. However, this physician represents an institution and it is a document of the institution, so we couldn't, as suggested by the Prosecution, pursuant to Rule 92 bis, examine or take a statement from this witness. This is the Military Medical Academy and this is a document of that institution. Also, in the Halilovic case, there is a decision of the 16th of February, 2005, where there is no prohibition on the admission of documents, only on the ground that the author has not been asked to testify. However, on the transcript pages of the 10th and 11th of April, Witness P018 also commented on these circumstances. In this way, Witness P018 is not placed in an unfair position because he did comment on the documents and the circumstances that the documents reflect and which we are trying to have admitted into evidence. He was not only shown what is written in the documents, but on page 7523, dated the 11th of April, 2006, we asked him as follows: "You also said that you were sent to the Military Medical Academy for an examination with a neuropsychiatrist because everyone thought that you were crazy." And he said, "Yes." Then I asked him: "Thank you. Let me tell you now, with respect to your visit during the Vukovar operation, that, in fact, you were never there. You made this whole thing up." And his answer -- you have his answer. And then, finally, on behalf of the Defence, I said to this witness, P018: "I am submitting, once again, that you were not at the academy in connection with the killing of Sostic, of Lieutenant Sostic. He was killed as soon as he reached Vukovar, although he claimed that it was much later. Secondly, his body was not dismembered, that you had to carry him in a blanket. He had a shrapnel wound in the head. Thirdly, he was pulled out by other soldiers with the help of the captain. And fourthly, and most importantly, the Defence has verified through their investigators that you went to the academy because of knee problems in February. You were on the 14th floor because you knew about this, but there is absolutely no indication that you were there during the Vukovar events. These are all pure fabrications. You have made this up and that is why you can't answer my question when you went there, who sent you there, who brought you there, how you went back," et cetera, et cetera. So the accused would be placed in an awkward position if the Court were not to be informed about these things to see that the witness did not speak the truth. The court files in the Serbian and Yugoslav law never had the status of confidential documents. These are all public documents. As for the document linked to Witness P018, the document under 65 ter 2(D)(iii), (vii), and it is underlined in the Prosecution's submission, paragraph 17, that the document is not dated, which the Defence interpreted as challenging the authenticity of that document. But what do I say to that? The Prosecutor cannot, at this stage, challenge the authenticity of their own document which they disclosed to the Defence. It was on the basis of that Prosecution document that we examined this witness. Also, from the Halilovic case, with respect to similar documents shown and tendered, it is stated that such documents don't have to be signed and stamped; they don't even have to have a date, and yet they can be considered authentic. Your Honours, the Defence submits that all these documents, particularly those relevant to Witness P024, that is, documents issued by judicial bodies, are documents with a high degree of probative value and are, therefore, relevant for judging not only the credibility of the witness but all the evidence which he produced and which he referred to in the course of his testimony and which are linked to the position of my client. All these court documents and judgements are considered reliable documents. The Prosecutor never challenged their authenticity; they have more possibilities to do that than myself. And if certain documents, such as the judgement and the indictment of Ovcara, support it without any reservations upon the tendering by the Prosecution, without checking them, believing that this would not undermine the fairness of the proceedings, without further comment, we feel that the Defence should enjoy a footing of equality with the Prosecution with respect to similar documents. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lunny.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With regard, first of all, to the documents relating to Witness P018, documents 2D36 and 2D37, as I understand it, my learned friend is now stating that an undertaking was given by my former colleague, Mr. Bill Smith. I am afraid I'm certainly unaware of any such undertaking, and it is regrettable that was not raised before today. Had that been mentioned in any earlier motion, then the matter could have been checked to make sure that we are talking about the same documents with regard to any undertaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that Witness P018 or P024?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: P018, Your Honour. And certainly the matter could have been checked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously, if any such undertaking was given, the Prosecution would be bound by that and would, indeed, stand by that. But we wish the opportunity to check the position, just to make sure we're talking about the documents. I'm not challenging my friend's integrity as an officer of the court, but just to make sure there is no confusion and there is no doubt that we are talking about documents 2D36 and 2D37. In the meantime, Your Honour, with regard to those documents, the Prosecution will stand by what was written in its motion of 25th of October. I don't think there's anything I can add beyond what was written in the Prosecution motion at that time. However, with regard to 2D36, I think my learned friend is maintaining that Rule 92 bis was not open to them, given the nature of the document. And the Prosecution would submit at this stage, again, that, on the face of it, it is a letter from a doctor, a named individual, to my learned friend's law firm stating a position contrary to Witness P018, and it seems to be no more than that. At this stage, it really is just a letter. On that basis, Your Honour, the Prosecution would underline and stress and further submit that Rule 92 bis would, indeed, be the correct way forward. With regard to Witness P024, Your Honour, the Prosecution, again, submits that the position set out in its written motion ought to be upheld and my friend's motion repelled. It would appear that the Defence came into the information on the evening of the 14th, which was during the cross-examination of Witness P024. There is now a challenge to Witness P024's credibility with regard to his answers, and I would submit that is not a fair position to put to that witness now, in a vacuum. The witness was challenged with a series of dates and a series of reference numbers which may, in fairness, giving the benefit of the doubt, may have meant nothing to him. We just simply do not know what his answer might have been if he had been shown the documents and allowed a chance to comment on those documents. However, he was simply confronted with a series of dates and numbers. To jump to the conclusion that he is lying because of the answers he gave, I would respectfully submit, is a step too far, without allowing that witness the fairness of seeing the documents and having them placed before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean you propose the witness should be recalled?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was the position taken within the Prosecution's written response of the 25th of October, and the Prosecution would stand by that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Anything else, Mr. Lunny?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: Not really, Your Honour. Just to say, generally, within common law, matters of credibility are final. There is a remedy open to my friend to recall witnesses and I would submit that is the proper course, should he wish to do that, rather than leave matters in a vacuum, which is not fair to the witnesses in question. Unless there's anything further, Your Honour, that requires our assistance, I do not wish to say anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUNNY
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. I sent this document to the Prosecution, showing my communication with Mr. Smith; however, that's irrelevant now. If the Prosecution proposes that we recall Witness P024 in order to examine him about these judicial documents, I will gladly do that. I simply didn't wish to waste the Court's time. If that is the only option available, then I will accept it. But I initially thought that that wasn't necessary because this Trial Chamber is fully capable of assessing the validity of judicial documents and everything that I put to this witness at the time. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will reserve its decision in respect of both documents, allowing to the Prosecution in respect of the reliance upon the undertaking of Mr. Smith a week to consider the position and advise both Mr. Borovic and the Chamber of the outcome of its consideration. While we're interrupting the flow of the evidence, there was a motion in the course of the cross-examination of Mr. Sljivancanin by Mr. Moore for the admission into evidence of two statements made by Mr. Sljivancanin; one was a statement taken in February of 1998 by officers, it seems, of the security organ of the military in Belgrade; the other appears, essentially, a record of evidence or a statement made to an investigating judge in the military court late in the year 1998. The Chamber gave an extensive decision in respect of this matter, which is dated the 9th of October, 2006, in which we indicated that it would allow the use of each of those statements for limited and specific purposes, which is what Mr. Moore did in the course of the hearing, but would not admit either of those statements as evidence in the case so that they would not stand as substantive evidence against Mr. Sljivancanin. The Chamber is not persuaded by the submissions of Mr. Moore that the circumstances are now materially different in that Mr. Sljivancanin has now given evidence and has been cross-examined, in accordance with the Chamber's earlier order, on those statements. It appears to the Chamber that the objections to the admission of each of those statements as substantive evidence in this case remain of the significance that they had earlier, and for that reason, the Chamber is not prepared to admit either of these documents as substantive evidence in the trial. The Chamber will make use of the two statements in the manner indicated in its decision of the 9th of October, 2006. Now, Mr. Lukic, we've taken a fair bit of your time with your next witness. We would, because of the tapes, need to finish 50 minutes from now. Is that acceptable to you, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Our witness is ready to come into the courtroom and we can begin. What is certain is that, within the time remaining for today's work, which is 50 minutes, we will not be able to complete the examination of this witness. So it is up to you whether we should begin or not. We are in your hands, both we and our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are in yours and you are in ours, Mr. Bulatovic. We have in mind the desire to finish the case of Mr. Sljivancanin by a certain date. If you are happy that you can do that, we would allow you to commence the evidence on Monday. But if you think time is a real pressure, we'll commence the evidence now. Perhaps you and Mr. Lukic could discuss and let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case, upon my consultation with lead counsel, Mr. Lukic, I think it would be better if we started on Monday, and I think Mr. Sljivancanin would need a rest as well. And I hear that other counsel feel the same, except for Mr. Borovic, but he has to go with the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Some people are blessed with a superior stamina, perhaps, Mr. Bulatovic. Well, in view of that encouraging indication, I think we would be better calling it an early day this Friday, with a view to a fresh start on Monday afternoon, at 2.15. I hope you all feel much more rested by then. We will, therefore, adjourn until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 6th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.44 p.m.,
